---
title: "Databases, repositories, identifiers, and versions"

---

# 1. Where should my data live?

You are preparing a manuscript about past ocean temperatures using coral geochemistry. To put your new measurements in context, you have queried existing paleoclimate records through [**LiPDGraph**](https://linkedearth.graphdb.mint.isi.edu).

Your new dataset is in [**LiPD (Linked Paleo Data)**](https://lipd.net/) format. It contains geochemical measurements, age information, site locations, and the information needed to interpret those measurements. You are ready to share the dataset associated with your paper.

**Where should you preserve the published dataset so that other researchers can find and retrieve it years from now?**

Explore the five possible destinations below. For each one, make an initial decision about whether it should be your **primary long-term archive**, then reveal what it actually offers. This is a decision-making exercise, not a scored quiz.

<section id="pond-d4-publish" aria-label="Choosing where to archive a coral dataset">
  <p class="pond-d4-progress" id="pond-d4-progress" aria-live="polite">0 of 5 destinations explored</p>
  <div id="pond-d4-cards" class="pond-d4-grid"></div>
  <div class="pond-d4-summary" id="pond-d4-summary" hidden>
    <p><strong>What did you notice?</strong> An appropriate archival repository might be disciplinary (like NOAA Paleoclimatology) or general-purpose (like Zenodo). A resource such as LiPDGraph provides valuable ways to discover and query data, but is not itself the long-term archive. The same dataset can therefore have an <strong>archival home</strong> and a separate <strong>discovery/query home</strong>.</p>
  </div>
</section>

<script>
(() => {
  const root = document.getElementById('pond-d4-publish');
  if (!root || root.dataset.initialized === 'true') return;
  root.dataset.initialized = 'true';

  // These are real destinations; the coral dataset in the scenario is hypothetical.
  const destinations = [
    {
      id: 'noaa',
      name: 'NOAA Paleoclimatology',
      preview: 'Maintained by NOAA, this specialized repository provides long-term archival, discovery, and access to paleoclimate datasets contributed by researchers around the world.',
      verdict: 'Strong archival choice for this dataset',
      explanation: 'NOAA’s World Data Service for Paleoclimatology is a domain repository: its scope, contribution process, and discovery tools are designed for paleoclimate research.',
      nuance: 'NOAA accepts LiPD files in addition to its NOAA contribution template. The same service also provides searchable access to archived data—so archival and database functions can overlap.',
      url: 'https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/access/paleo-search/',
      linkLabel: 'Explore NOAA Paleoclimatology'
    },
    {
      id: 'zenodo',
      name: 'Zenodo',
      preview: 'A general-purpose research repository that accepts data and other research outputs across disciplines.',
      verdict: 'A legitimate general-purpose archive',
      explanation: 'Zenodo preserves deposited research outputs and provides persistent identifiers. It could be a suitable archival home when an appropriate domain repository is unavailable or unsuitable.',
      nuance: 'For this coral dataset, NOAA may offer more relevant disciplinary discovery and curation. General-purpose does not mean inferior; repository choice depends on the data and the research community.',
      url: 'https://zenodo.org/',
      linkLabel: 'Explore Zenodo'
    },
    {
      id: 'lipdgraph',
      name: 'LiPDGraph',
      preview: 'A knowledge graph used to search and query paleoclimate records represented in LiPD.',
      verdict: 'Valuable database, not the archival home',
      explanation: 'LiPDGraph makes it possible to work with records across studies—for example, finding coral records that meet particular scientific criteria. That makes it useful for discovery and analysis.',
      nuance: 'But it is not designed to be the long-term archival repository for the dataset. Preserve the published dataset at an appropriate archive such as NOAA, even if it is also represented in LiPDGraph.',
      url: 'https://linked.earth/FreqFun/a-query-lipd-graph/',
      linkLabel: 'See an example LiPDGraph query'
    },
    {
      id: 'github',
      name: 'GitHub',
      preview: 'A platform for collaborating on files, documenting work, and tracking changes over time.',
      verdict: 'Useful alongside an archive, not by itself',
      explanation: 'GitHub can be helpful while developing a dataset or sharing the processing workflow. Its version-control features are valuable, but a GitHub repository alone is not a dedicated long-term data archive.',
      nuance: 'GitHub can be connected to Zenodo to archive a release. That is an example of using a working platform and an archival repository together.',
      url: 'https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/archiving-a-github-repository/referencing-and-citing-content',
      linkLabel: 'How GitHub links to an archive'
    },
    {
      id: 'labsite',
      name: 'Your lab website',
      preview: 'A project page where your research team can publish descriptions, figures, and downloadable files.',
      verdict: 'Useful project page, not enough on its own',
      explanation: 'A lab website can make the dataset visible to collaborators and readers, but the site may change or disappear as a project ends or people move institutions.',
      nuance: 'Link the page to an archival record at NOAA or another suitable repository. Researchers can then find the dataset through your site without depending on it as the only copy.',
      url: '',
      linkLabel: ''
    }
  ];

  const cards = root.querySelector('#pond-d4-cards');
  const progress = root.querySelector('#pond-d4-progress');
  const summary = root.querySelector('#pond-d4-summary');
  const explored = new Set();
  const labels = { yes: 'Yes', no: 'No', unsure: 'Not sure' };

  for (const [index, destination] of destinations.entries()) {
    const article = document.createElement('article');
    article.className = 'pond-d4-card';
    article.innerHTML = `
      <div class="pond-d4-inner">
        <div class="pond-d4-face pond-d4-front">
          <div class="pond-d4-kicker">Destination ${index + 1} of ${destinations.length}</div>
          <h3>${destination.name}</h3>
          <p class="pond-d4-intro">${destination.preview}</p>
          <div class="pond-d4-spacer"></div>
          <fieldset>
            <legend>Would you use this as the main long-term archive?</legend>
            <div class="pond-d4-choices" role="group" aria-label="Archive decision for ${destination.name}">
              <button type="button" class="pond-d4-choice" data-choice="yes" aria-pressed="false">Yes</button>
              <button type="button" class="pond-d4-choice" data-choice="no" aria-pressed="false">No</button>
              <button type="button" class="pond-d4-choice" data-choice="unsure" aria-pressed="false">Not sure</button>
            </div>
          </fieldset>
          <p class="pond-d4-status" aria-live="polite">Choose an option to reveal.</p>
          <button type="button" class="pond-d4-button pond-d4-reveal" disabled>Reveal what it provides</button>
        </div>
        <div class="pond-d4-face pond-d4-back" inert>
          <div class="pond-d4-kicker">What this destination offers</div>
          <h3>${destination.name}</h3>
          <p class="pond-d4-my-answer">Your initial thought: <strong class="pond-d4-answer"></strong></p>
          <p class="pond-d4-verdict">${destination.verdict}</p>
          <p>${destination.explanation}</p>
          <p>${destination.nuance}</p>
          ${destination.url ? `<a class="pond-d4-link" href="${destination.url}" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer">${destination.linkLabel}</a>` : ''}
          <div class="pond-d4-spacer"></div>
          <button type="button" class="pond-d4-button pond-d4-button-secondary pond-d4-back-button">Back to my choice</button>
        </div>
      </div>`;

    const front = article.querySelector('.pond-d4-front');
    const back = article.querySelector('.pond-d4-back');
    const reveal = article.querySelector('.pond-d4-reveal');
    const returnButton = article.querySelector('.pond-d4-back-button');
    const status = article.querySelector('.pond-d4-status');
    const answer = article.querySelector('.pond-d4-answer');
    let choice = null;

    article.querySelectorAll('[data-choice]').forEach(button => {
      button.addEventListener('click', () => {
        choice = button.dataset.choice;
        article.querySelectorAll('[data-choice]').forEach(other => {
          other.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(other === button));
        });
        status.textContent = 'Your choice is saved. Reveal to compare it with the platform’s role.';
        reveal.disabled = false;
      });
    });

    reveal.addEventListener('click', () => {
      if (choice === null) return;
      answer.textContent = labels[choice];
      front.inert = true;
      back.inert = false;
      article.classList.add('is-flipped');
      explored.add(destination.id);
      progress.textContent = `${explored.size} of ${destinations.length} destinations explored`;
      summary.hidden = explored.size !== destinations.length;
      returnButton.focus({ preventScroll: true });
    });

    returnButton.addEventListener('click', () => {
      back.inert = true;
      front.inert = false;
      article.classList.remove('is-flipped');
      reveal.focus({ preventScroll: true });
    });

    cards.appendChild(article);
  }
})();
</script>
```

# 2. Can someone reproduce my analysis five years later?

You are studying nitrate concentrations in a river. Your measurements come from a **live water-quality database**: researchers add new observations regularly and sometimes correct older records. You query the database for observations collected **between 2015 and 2025** and use the results in a manuscript submitted in **2026**.

You documented the database name, your access date, and the exact query. **Will that be enough for another researcher to retrieve the same values in 2031?**

Try the small simulation below. The database and observations are **fictional**; the changes illustrate what can happen in a real, continuously updated database.

<section id="pond-d4-retrace"
         aria-label="Reproducing an analysis from a changing database">

  <!-- STEP 1: RE-RUN THE QUERY -->
  <div class="pond-a2-panel">

    <h3>Step 1 — Re-run your original query</h3>

    <p class="pond-a2-small">
      In January 2026, you downloaded the records needed for your
      paper. Below are four example rows from that extract,
      not the entire dataset.
    </p>

    <div class="pond-a2-query" aria-label="Query settings">
      <span>Variable: nitrate (mg N/L)</span>
      <span>Stations: UP-01, MID-02, DW-03</span>
      <span>Dates: 2015–2025</span>
    </div>

    <div class="pond-a2-table-wrap">
      <table>
        <caption class="pond-a2-sr-only">
          Example nitrate observations from the 2026 analysis
          extract compared with the same query in 2031

        database maintainers corrected historical observations.
        The 2015–2025 date filter excluded new observations collected
        after 2025, but it could not undo corrections to older records.
      </p>

      <p>
        Knowing that you accessed the database in January 2026
        tells others <em>when</em> you retrieved the data.

            <p>
              However, the same query against a changing database

            <div class="pond-a2-flip-spacer"></div>

            <button type="button"
                    class="pond-a2-button pond-a2-button-secondary pond-a2-flip-close">

      <!-- CARD 2: ARCHIVE THE ANALYSIS DATASET -->

            </div>

            <h4>Archive the analysis dataset</h4>

            <div class="pond-a2-flip-kicker">

            </div>

            <h4>Preserves the values actually used</h4>

            <p>
              A fixed, archived extract lets someone retrieve
              the original observations even after the live
              database has changed.
            </p>

            <p>
              Paired with your documented query, it preserves
              both <strong>what you used</strong> and
              <strong>how you obtained it</strong>.
              This can satisfy the preservation requirement
              without a separate archived database release.
            </p>

            <div class="pond-a2-flip-spacer"></div>

            <button type="button"
                    class="pond-a2-button pond-a2-button-secondary pond-a2-flip-close">

              What it contributes
            </div>

            <h4>Preserves a fixed state of the database</h4>

            <p>
              If the 2026 release is genuinely archived,
              immutable, and retrievable, a future researcher
              can apply your documented query to that release
              to recover the original observations.
            </p>

            <p>
              The database then serves an
              <strong>archival function</strong> too.
              A live homepage or access date alone would
              not provide this guarantee.
            </p>

            <div class="pond-a2-flip-spacer"></div>

            <button type="button"
                    class="pond-a2-button pond-a2-button-secondary pond-a2-flip-close">

         hidden

      <p>
        <strong>What is the minimum?</strong>
        Always document the database, access date, and exact
        query or selection criteria. You also need a reliable
        way to retrieve the values used in the paper:
        <strong>either</strong> an archived analysis dataset
        <strong>or</strong> a preserved, identifiable database
        release from which those values can be recovered.
      </p>

      <p>
        Both archival routes can be useful, but you do not
        necessarily need both. The important thing is that
        the original data remain identifiable and
        retrievable—not merely available through today's
        live database.
      </p>
    </div>

</section>

<script>
(() => {
  const root = document.getElementById('pond-d4-retrace');

  if (!root || root.dataset.initialized === 'true') return;
  root.dataset.initialized = 'true';

  const runButton = root.querySelector('#pond-a2-run');
  const drift = root.querySelector('#pond-a2-drift');
  const recovery = root.querySelector('#pond-a2-recovery');

  // Step 1: Re-run the original query
  runButton.addEventListener('click', () => {

    root.querySelectorAll('.pond-a2-later').forEach(cell => {
      cell.hidden = false;
    });

    drift.hidden = false;
    root.querySelector('#pond-a2-mobile-hint').hidden = false;
    recovery.hidden = false;

    runButton.disabled = true;
    runButton.textContent = '2031 results shown';

    drift.focus({ preventScroll: true });
  });

  // Step 2: Explore the flip cards
  // No right/wrong answers or scoring

  const progress = root.querySelector('#pond-a2-progress');
  const summary = root.querySelector('#pond-a2-summary');

  const explored = new Set();
  const cards = root.querySelectorAll('.pond-a2-flip-card');

  cards.forEach(card => {

    const front = card.querySelector('.pond-a2-flip-front');
    const back = card.querySelector('.pond-a2-flip-back');

    const reveal = card.querySelector('.pond-a2-flip-open');
    const returnButton = card.querySelector('.pond-a2-flip-close');

    reveal.addEventListener('click', () => {

      front.inert = true;
      back.inert = false;

      card.classList.add('is-flipped');

      explored.add(card.dataset.practice);

      progress.textContent =
        `${explored.size} of ${cards.length} practices explored`;

      summary.hidden = explored.size !== cards.length;

      returnButton.focus({ preventScroll: true });
    });

    returnButton.addEventListener('click', () => {

      back.inert = true;
      front.inert = false;

      card.classList.remove('is-flipped');

      reveal.focus({ preventScroll: true });
    });
  });
})();
</script>
```

**What matters here?** A live database may be the best place to explore current observations. **Always document the exact query and selection criteria**, as well as the source and access date. But to reproduce a published result, another researcher also needs a way to retrieve the **state of the data actually used**: an archived analysis extract or an identifiable, preserved database release.

In the next activity, we'll look more closely at how datasets change between **releases** and why identifying the specific version matters.

# 3. Which dataset did I actually use?

A research team has published a **coastal temperature dataset** in an archival repository. The dataset is useful, but it is not static: the team corrects a station location and later discovers that some temperatures must be recalibrated.

You are preparing a manuscript in **2026** using this dataset. It already has more than one release, and further corrections may follow. **How will someone reading your manuscript in 2031 retrieve the exact data you analyzed?**

Explore the release history and then investigate different ways to identify a data product. **The project, releases, and measurements below are fictional.**

          </div>
          <div class="pond-a3-flip-face pond-a3-flip-back" inert>
            <div class="pond-a3-flip-kicker">What it contributes</div>
            <h4>Names a file, not a release</h4>
            <p>A filename can help identify a file within an archive, but the same
              name might appear in multiple releases. “Final” does not mean
              permanent.</p>
            <p>Pair the filename with a <strong>preserved, identifiable release</strong>
              so readers can retrieve the right copy.</p>
            <div class="pond-a3-flip-spacer"></div>
            <button type="button" class="pond-a3-button pond-a3-button-secondary pond-a3-flip-close">Back to card</button>
          </div>
        </div>
      </article>

      <!-- CARD 2: LAB URL -->
      <article class="pond-a3-flip-card" data-reference="lab">
        <div class="pond-a3-flip-inner">
          <div class="pond-a3-flip-face pond-a3-flip-front">
            <div class="pond-a3-flip-kicker">Reference 2</div>
            <h4>Lab website URL</h4>
            <p>A link to the research group's data page.</p>
            <p class="pond-a3-flip-hint">Will the link still lead to your release later?</p>
            <div class="pond-a3-flip-spacer"></div>
            <button type="button" class="pond-a3-button pond-a3-flip-open">Reveal what it contributes</button>
          </div>
          <div class="pond-a3-flip-face pond-a3-flip-back" inert>
            <div class="pond-a3-flip-kicker">What it contributes</div>
            <h4>Helps people find the project</h4>
            <p>A lab page can explain the research and link to archived releases.
              But its address or contents may change, and it may only offer
              the newest file.</p>
            <p>Use it for context or discovery, <strong>not as the only way</strong>
              to locate the preserved release.</p>
            <div class="pond-a3-flip-spacer"></div>
            <button type="button" class="pond-a3-button pond-a3-button-secondary pond-a3-flip-close">Back to card</button>
          </div>
        </div>
      </article>

      <!-- CARD 3: REPOSITORY LANDING PAGE -->
      <article class="pond-a3-flip-card" data-reference="landing">
        <div class="pond-a3-flip-inner">
          <div class="pond-a3-flip-face pond-a3-flip-front">
            <div class="pond-a3-flip-kicker">Reference 3</div>
            <h4>Repository landing page</h4>
            <p>A page in the archive listing the dataset and its releases.</p>
            <p class="pond-a3-flip-hint">Does it lead to the dataset or to your exact release?</p>
            <div class="pond-a3-flip-spacer"></div>
            <button type="button" class="pond-a3-button pond-a3-flip-open">Reveal what it contributes</button>
          </div>
          <div class="pond-a3-flip-face pond-a3-flip-back" inert>
            <div class="pond-a3-flip-kicker">What it contributes</div>
            <h4>Connects readers to archived records</h4>
            <p>A general dataset page may list several releases or emphasize
              the newest one, so readers may still have to find your version.</p>
            <p>A <strong>stable page for a specific archived release</strong>,
              with a permanent record identifier, can identify exactly what
              you used—even without a DOI for each version.</p>
            <div class="pond-a3-flip-spacer"></div>
            <button type="button" class="pond-a3-button pond-a3-button-secondary pond-a3-flip-close">Back to card</button>
          </div>
        </div>
      </article>

      <!-- CARD 4: DATASET-LEVEL DOI -->
      <article class="pond-a3-flip-card" data-reference="concept">
        <div class="pond-a3-flip-inner">
          <div class="pond-a3-flip-face pond-a3-flip-front">
            <div class="pond-a3-flip-kicker">Reference 4</div>
            <h4>Dataset-level persistent identifier</h4>
            <p>For example, a <em>concept DOI</em> representing the dataset across releases.</p>
            <p class="pond-a3-flip-hint">What happens when a newer version is published?</p>
            <div class="pond-a3-flip-spacer"></div>
            <button type="button" class="pond-a3-button pond-a3-flip-open">Reveal what it contributes</button>
          </div>
          <div class="pond-a3-flip-face pond-a3-flip-back" inert>
            <div class="pond-a3-flip-kicker">What it contributes</div>
            <h4>Identifies the evolving dataset</h4>
            <p>A persistent identifier can continue to direct readers to a
              managed record even if its website address changes.</p>
            <p>A concept DOI represents <strong>all releases</strong>, not
              necessarily the one analyzed. Readers may still need an
              explicit version or release-specific record.</p>
            <div class="pond-a3-flip-spacer"></div>
            <button type="button" class="pond-a3-button pond-a3-button-secondary pond-a3-flip-close">Back to card</button>
          </div>
        </div>
      </article>

      <!-- CARD 5: VERSION-SPECIFIC DOI -->
      <article class="pond-a3-flip-card" data-reference="version">
        <div class="pond-a3-flip-inner">
          <div class="pond-a3-flip-face pond-a3-flip-front">
            <div class="pond-a3-flip-kicker">Reference 5</div>
            <h4>Version-specific persistent identifier</h4>
            <p>For example, a DOI assigned to one particular archived release.</p>
            <p class="pond-a3-flip-hint">How would this help a future reader?</p>
            <div class="pond-a3-flip-spacer"></div>
            <button type="button" class="pond-a3-button pond-a3-flip-open">Reveal what it contributes</button>
          </div>
          <div class="pond-a3-flip-face pond-a3-flip-back" inert>
            <div class="pond-a3-flip-kicker">What it contributes</div>
            <h4>Points to one identifiable release</h4>
            <p>A version-specific DOI can direct readers to the archived
              record for exactly the release you used, even if the
              repository's web address changes.</p>
            <p>It is a strong option <strong>when available</strong>, but
              not the only one. An unambiguous, permanent repository record
              plus an explicit version can also work.</p>
            <div class="pond-a3-flip-spacer"></div>
            <button type="button" class="pond-a3-button pond-a3-button-secondary pond-a3-flip-close">Back to card</button>
          </div>
        </div>
      </article>

    </div>

    <div class="pond-a3-synthesis" id="pond-a3-synthesis" hidden aria-live="polite">
      <p><strong>What is the minimum?</strong> Someone must be able to
        <strong>unambiguously identify and retrieve the exact archived release</strong>
        used in your analysis. A specific version DOI is a convenient way to
        do this, but a stable archival record identifier together with the
        version can also meet this goal.</p>
      <p>Other references still have roles: a filename identifies files within
        the release; a lab page helps discovery; and a dataset-level DOI
        links the releases together. The identifier by itself does not
        preserve the data—the repository does that.</p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<script>
(() => {
  const root = document.getElementById('pond-d4-versions');
  if (!root || root.dataset.initialized === 'true') return;
  root.dataset.initialized = 'true';

  const releases = {
    v1: {
      title: 'Version 1.0 · Initial release',
      detail: 'The research team publishes its first archived dataset. The measurements and station locations below are used as originally reported.',
      lat1: '44.10', lat2: '44.60', temp1: '12.4', temp2: '11.8',
      changed: [],
      note: 'This is the baseline release. There are no earlier archived changes to compare.'
    },
    v11: {
      title: 'Version 1.1 · Corrected station coordinates',
      detail: 'A location error is found for station CT-02. The team corrects its latitude, documents the change, and preserves the original version 1.0. The temperature readings have not changed.',
      lat1: '44.10', lat2: '44.68', temp1: '12.4', temp2: '11.8',
      changed: ['lat2'],
      note: 'Changed since 1.0: CT-02 latitude, from 44.60°N to 44.68°N. This might change which region a spatial analysis assigns to that station.'
    },
    v2: {
      title: 'Version 2.0 · Recalibrated temperatures',
      detail: 'The team discovers an instrument calibration issue and recalculates the temperature estimates. The corrected station coordinates from version 1.1 are retained. Earlier releases remain archived.',
      lat1: '44.10', lat2: '44.68', temp1: '12.1', temp2: '11.5',
      changed: ['temp1', 'temp2'],
      note: 'Changed since 1.1: CT-01 temperature, from 12.4°C to 12.1°C, and CT-02 temperature, from 11.8°C to 11.5°C. A reanalysis might produce a different scientific result.'
    }
  };

  const visited = new Set(['v1']);
  const cells = {
    lat1: root.querySelector('#pond-a3-lat1'),
    lat2: root.querySelector('#pond-a3-lat2'),
    temp1: root.querySelector('#pond-a3-temp1'),
    temp2: root.querySelector('#pond-a3-temp2')
  };

  root.querySelectorAll('.pond-a3-release').forEach(button => {
    button.addEventListener('click', () => {
      const version = button.dataset.version;
      const data = releases[version];
      visited.add(version);
      root.querySelectorAll('.pond-a3-release').forEach(b => {
        b.setAttribute('aria-pressed', String(b === button));
      });
      root.querySelector('#pond-a3-release-title').textContent = data.title;
      root.querySelector('#pond-a3-release-detail').textContent = data.detail;
      root.querySelector('#pond-a3-change-note').textContent = data.note;
      Object.entries(cells).forEach(([key, cell]) => {
        cell.textContent = data[key];
        cell.classList.toggle('pond-a3-changed', data.changed.includes(key));
      });
      root.querySelector('#pond-a3-archive-note').hidden = visited.size < 3;
    });
  });

  // Step 2: explore the references. No scoring or single correct choice.
  const progress = root.querySelector('#pond-a3-progress');
  const synthesis = root.querySelector('#pond-a3-synthesis');
  const explored = new Set();
  const cards = root.querySelectorAll('.pond-a3-flip-card');

  cards.forEach(card => {
    const front = card.querySelector('.pond-a3-flip-front');
    const back = card.querySelector('.pond-a3-flip-back');
    const open = card.querySelector('.pond-a3-flip-open');
    const close = card.querySelector('.pond-a3-flip-close');

    open.addEventListener('click', () => {
      front.inert = true;
      back.inert = false;
      card.classList.add('is-flipped');
      explored.add(card.dataset.reference);
      progress.textContent =
        `${explored.size} of ${cards.length} references explored`;
      synthesis.hidden = explored.size !== cards.length;
      close.focus({ preventScroll: true });
    });

    close.addEventListener('click', () => {
      back.inert = true;
      front.inert = false;
      card.classList.remove('is-flipped');
      open.focus({ preventScroll: true });
    });
  });
})();
</script>
```

**What matters here?** A dataset can change, and those changes may affect scientific conclusions. For reproducibility, preserve the release history and identify the **exact archived version used in the analysis**. A persistent identifier helps others find that research object in the future, but only if the record and data behind it remain preserved. We'll return to how to **cite data in a manuscript** in the last [LilyPad](../citing-data/index.qmd).

# 4. One dataset, two homes

Let's return to the **coral geochemistry dataset** from Activity 1. Imagine the team has now archived the published dataset with **NOAA Paleoclimatology** and also made its LiPD records available through **LiPDGraph**.

The *same scientific study* can be available through both services, but the services are not interchangeable. **Which home would help with each task?** Think about it, then flip the cards to explore what each service contributes. There are no scored answers.

*This is a fictional publication scenario using two real scientific services; it does not imply that an actual dataset has been deposited or automatically synchronized between them.*

<section id="pond-d4-twohomes" aria-label="One dataset, two complementary data homes">

  <div class="pond-a4-homes" aria-label="The two services in this scenario">
    <div class="pond-a4-home">
      <span class="pond-a4-home-tag">Archival home</span>
      <strong>NOAA Paleoclimatology</strong>
      <p>Preserves contributed paleoclimate datasets, with archival records, discovery tools, and DOIs.</p>
    </div>
    <div class="pond-a4-home">
      <span class="pond-a4-home-tag">Additional access and query service</span>

  <p class="pond-a4-progress" id="pond-a4-progress" aria-live="polite">0 of 4 situations explored</p>

  <div class="pond-a4-grid">

    <!-- Situation 1: both services offer discovery, in different ways -->
    <article class="pond-a4-card" data-situation="discover">
      <div class="pond-a4-inner">
        <div class="pond-a4-face pond-a4-front">

          <h3>Retrieve the exact data used in the paper</h3>
          <p>The database's available records may have changed since the manuscript was published.</p>
          <p>What allows a new researcher to recover the original data?</p>
          <div class="pond-a4-spacer"></div>
          <button type="button" class="pond-a4-button pond-a4-open">Reveal the possibilities</button>
        </div>
        <div class="pond-a4-face pond-a4-back" inert>

          <h3>Return to the archived state</h3>
          <p class="pond-a4-support"><strong>NOAA:</strong> Retrieve the identifiable archived data product used for the paper, provided that specific release was preserved.</p>
          <p class="pond-a4-support"><strong>LiPDGraph:</strong> Useful for querying, including potentially a frozen graph version, but it is not the long-term archival substitute.</p>
          <p><strong>Notice:</strong> Document how you selected the data, and preserve the specific data state you used.</p>
          <div class="pond-a4-spacer"></div>
          <button type="button" class="pond-a4-button pond-a4-button-secondary pond-a4-close">Back to situation</button>

    </article>

  </div>

  <div class="pond-a4-synthesis" id="pond-a4-synthesis" hidden aria-live="polite">
    <p><strong>One dataset, two homes.</strong> NOAA Paleoclimatology is the dataset's <strong>archival home</strong>. LiPDGraph offers another way to discover, query, and work with records. Their functions overlap, especially for discovery and access, but long-term preservation must be provided by a service with appropriate archival commitments.</p>
    <p><strong>Minimum requirement:</strong> The data product used in a publication must be preserved in an appropriate repository and remain unambiguously identifiable and retrievable. Other services can make the same data more useful without replacing that archive.</p>
  </div>

</section>

<script>
(() => {
  const root = document.getElementById('pond-d4-twohomes');
  if (!root || root.dataset.initialized === 'true') return;
  root.dataset.initialized = 'true';

  const explored = new Set();
  const cards = root.querySelectorAll('.pond-a4-card');
  const progress = root.querySelector('#pond-a4-progress');
  const synthesis = root.querySelector('#pond-a4-synthesis');

  cards.forEach(card => {
    const front = card.querySelector('.pond-a4-front');
    const back = card.querySelector('.pond-a4-back');
    const reveal = card.querySelector('.pond-a4-open');
    const close = card.querySelector('.pond-a4-close');

    reveal.addEventListener('click', () => {
      front.inert = true;
      back.inert = false;
      card.classList.add('is-flipped');
      explored.add(card.dataset.situation);
      progress.textContent = `${explored.size} of ${cards.length} situations explored`;
      synthesis.hidden = explored.size !== cards.length;
      close.focus({ preventScroll: true });
    });

    close.addEventListener('click', () => {
      back.inert = true;
      front.inert = false;
      card.classList.remove('is-flipped');
      reveal.focus({ preventScroll: true });
    });
  });
})();
</script>
```

**Key takeaway:** Publishing data means more than uploading a file. Preserve the published data product in an appropriate repository, give others a reliable way to identify the specific version, and use complementary services—such as databases—to make it easier to discover and work with the data. **A database can also serve as the archival home if it genuinely provides those preservation guarantees.**

In [the next LilyPad](../sharing-data/index.qmd), we'll focus on preparing data for sharing and reuse; in [the last LilyPad](../citing-data/index.qmd), we'll practice citing datasets in manuscripts. For a look at the real services behind this example, explore [NOAA's guidance for contributing paleoclimate data](https://www.ncei.noaa.gov/products/paleoclimatology/contributing-data) and [the LiPDGraph querying tutorial](https://linked.earth/pylipdTutorials/notebooks/L2_b_using_graphdb.html).
